caption:
India's IT majors are redesigning their offices, and RTO mandates keep tightening through this quarter. That changes what you're judged on.

For years the work spoke in a chat window. Deliverables, documents, a green dot. In a room, the ledger is different. Who holds the floor. Who yields it. Who speaks after the interruption and who never comes back to the point.

There is no raise-hand button in a conference room. There is bearing. There is tone. There is the pause you take before you answer, which most people fill with noise because silence makes them uncomfortable.

Three things to carry in on Monday:

Sit so your shoulders face the person speaking. Posture is read before you open your mouth.

When you're cut off, stop. Let them finish. Then take your sentence from the top, same words, lower pace.

Answer one beat late. A deliberate pause reads as command. A rushed answer reads as permission-seeking.

The room is back. Learn to hold it.

topic.title: Return-to-office redesign makes physical presence visible again
topic.angle: After years of being judged on deliverables in a chat window, this audience is back in rooms where bearing, pauses and interruptions decide who gets believed — and there's no raise-hand button.
topic.why_now: Coverage of India's IT majors redesigning offices published roughly a week ago, and RTO mandates are tightening through the final quarter, catching people in the short transition window where they're still conscious of how they show up.

rationale: A stark text-only visual matches the no-nonsense, command-authority tone and lets the single hard line about the missing raise-hand button carry the whole return-to-office argument.
